Q-RTS: a real-time swarm intelligence based
on multi-agent Q-learning
M. Matta✉, G.C. Cardarilli, L. Di Nunzio, R. Fazzolari,
D. Giardino, M. Re, F. Silvestri and S. Spanò
The authors introduce a novel approach for swarm reinforcement
learning that extends the standard Q-learning to multi-agent systems.
State-of-the-art methods implement a knowledge sharing mechanism
between the agents that is triggered by the episodes succession. This
causes an intrinsic limit in the convergence speed of the algorithms.
They overcame this issue by developing a Q-learning real-time
swarm algorithm (Q-RTS), which is iteration-based and suitable for
real-time systems. Q-RTS was tested in different environments and
compared to other related methods in the literature. They obtained
positive results in terms of learning time and scalability, i.e. achieving
a speed-up factor of at least 1.49 with respect to standard Q-learning.
Moreover, Q-RTS shows enhanced learning performance as the
environments complexity increases.
Introduction: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an artiﬁcial intelligence
technique to train an agent to perform a task by interacting with
the environment. By trial-and-error, the agent adapts its behaviour
through a rewarding mechanism, called reinforcement, which is a
measure of its task-solving performance [1]. In recent years, RL
became increasingly popular in various ﬁelds, e.g. robotics [2], ﬁnancial
trading [3] and industrial applications [4].
In standard RL algorithms the environment is often modelled as a
Markovian decision process. The agents gather knowledge from the
environment through an exploration process: at time t, the agent in a
state st takes an action at according to a policy p and it observes the
changes in the environment dynamics. The information derived from
this reaction is the reward, which can be a stimulus or a deterrent. It

Introduction: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an arti fi cial intelligence technique to train an agent to perform a task by interacting with the environment. By trial-and-error, the agent adapts its behaviour through a rewarding mechanism, called reinforcement, which is a measure of its task-solving performance [ 1 ]. In recent years, RL became increasingly popular in various fi elds, e.g. robotics [ 2 ], fi nancial trading [ 3 ] and industrial applications [ 4 ]. In standard RL algorithms the environment is often modelled as a Markovian decision process. The agents gather knowledge from the environment through an exploration process: at time t , the agent in a state s t takes an action a t according to a policy p and it observes the changes in the environment dynamics. The information derived from this reaction is the reward, which can be a stimulus or a deterrent. It is used to update a state-value function that is a record of the expected return of the cumulative reward over time. Through the state-value func- tion V p ( s ), the agent learns the quality of its new state derived from doing a t when in s t following p . If the agent successfully completes a task, it reaches a terminal state s goal and concludes the current episode [ 1 ]. The next episode starts with an up-to-date state-value function which is exploited by the now expert agent. It explores the environment again, optimising its set of actions over time to reach the goal state and maximising the expected rewards. The use of an updated state-value function through the episodes is called knowledge exploitation. There are many RL algorithms and the most prominent example is Q-learning by Watkins [ 5 ]. RL algorithms for multi-agent systems are also present in the literature and they are often bio-inspired [ 6 ]. The agents are organised in ensembles, e.g. a swarm, with enhanced learning capabilities [ 7 ]. Coordination and knowledge sharing among the agents are key points in swarm RL. The literature proposes several methods for agent knowl- edge sharing that are based on the episodes succession [ 6 , 8 ]. In the cited works, the proposed RL algorithms trigger the information exchange whenever all the agents reach a goal state. Therefore, the update of an agent state-value function is unaffected by the swarm dynamics until the current episode of the last agent is complete. This episodic triggering is critical for the convergence time of the algorithm and causes a limit- ation in sight of a real-time implementation. In this Letter, we propose a swarm learning solution that overcomes the explained swarm RL algor- ithms timing limitations by making the knowledge sharing iteration- based. We introduce the Q-learning real-time swarm algorithm (Q-RTS), a modi fi ed version of Q-learning by Watkins, that is suitable for real-time RL of intelligent swarms. The purpose of such function is to emphasise the most valuable pieces of experience gathered by the agents during the iteration, both for positive and negative events. Experimental results: In this section, we provide some experimental results to verify the faster convergence of Q-RTS to the same numerical values computed using standard Q-learning. The action set A includes four position shifts: going up , right , down and left . In our experiments, the learning rate is a = 0 . 5, the discount factor g = 0 . 95, the action- selection policy is e - greedy with e = 0 . 2 and the independence factor is b = 0 . 1. All the Q i [ P are initialised as zero matrices. The agents gain r = 100 when they reach the goal position, r = − 0 . 1 for each step taken and they are discouraged with r = − 101 if they hit a wall. Each agent experiments its own episode succession: when the goal is reached, the local episode is concluded and the agent position is reset randomly. All the results presented in this section are referred to the mean values of 40 experiments with the same set of hyperpara- meters, which include the number of agents and the maze size and structure. In the fi rst set of experiments, we tested Q-RTS on mazes with random initial position and a fi xed goal cell. Fig. 2 represents the optimal solution for a maze of size 14 × 14, obtained using both Q-learning and Q-RTS with a variable number of agents. As shown in Fig. 3 , we observed a speedup in the convergence time based on the number of iterations to reach the optimal Q -values. Such values are the same obtained by Q-learning. The convergence speed increases as more agents are in the swarm. We tested Q-RTS also on mazes of sizes 9 × 9, 20 × 20, 30 × 30 and 40 × 40. The speedup values with respect to Q-learning are shown in Table 1 . We observed that the speedup values scale not only with the number of agents but also with the state-space dimension, i.e. the maze size. The speedup satur- ation in the cases 9 × 9 and 14 × 14 suggests that there is an optimal number of agents which depends on the complexity of the environment. This implies that Q-RTS obtains better results in applications with large state-spaces. We implemented extended pheronomone-Q method (PHE2-Q) which is based on ant colony optimisation (ACO) [ 9 ]. Swarms of four agents deployed using Q-RTS and PHE2-Q were tested in a 40 × 40 maze. The agents initial position and the goal cell were fi xed. As described in [ 8 ], the additional parameters of PHE2-Q were set as follows: initial value of pheromone evaporation rate r = 0 . 5, number of episodes for which the individual Q-learning is performed between two succes- sive information exchanges Y = 5. Fig. 4 compares the two algorithms in terms of the number of actions required to reach the goal as a function of iterations. We observed that both methods achieve the same minimum number of actions (96 in the test case) but Q-RTS requires less iterations than PHE2-Q to solve the maze and to converge towards the optimal solution.
